q: Goldstein gave which other name to the rays he saw passing through the holes of a perforated cathode?
x: Goldstein called them canal rays because they pass through the holes (canals) of a perforated cathode. Cathode rays are streams of electrons, not positive particles.

q: In an electric field, positive rays are deflected:
x: Positive rays are made of positively charged ions, so they are attracted towards the negative plate. Cathode rays bend the other way, towards the positive plate.

q: Compared with cathode rays in the same magnetic field, positive rays are deflected:
o: More, and in the opposite direction
Less, and in the opposite direction
Less, and in the same direction
More, and in the same direction
x: Positive ions are far heavier than electrons, so they bend much less; their charge is opposite, so they bend the opposite way.

q: The charge on a proton is:
x: A proton carries a positive charge of 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, equal in size to the electron's charge. The values 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ and 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ are masses in kg, not charges.

q: A light paddle wheel placed in the path of positive rays begins to rotate. This shows that positive rays:
o: Are a form of electromagnetic radiation
Consist of material particles that possess momentum
x: Turning the paddle wheel shows that the rays are made of particles with mass and velocity, i.e. momentum. Their deflection by fields shows separately that they are charged.

q: Goldstein could observe positive rays in his tube only under conditions of:
o: High gas pressure and low voltage
High gas pressure and high voltage
Low gas pressure and high voltage
Normal air pressure and no voltage
x: At low pressure and high voltage, cathode-ray electrons strike gas molecules and ionise them; the positive ions then stream towards the cathode.

q: Which two ions found in positive rays have the same e/m ratio? (H = 1, He = 4)
x: e/m of He²⁺ = 2/4 = 1/2 and of H₂⁺ = 1/2, so they are equal. H⁺ has 1/1, He⁺ has 1/4, so the other pairs differ.

q: The energy of a photon of wavelength λ is given by:
x: E = hν and ν = c/λ, so E = hc/λ. Energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.

q: A photon of which kind of electromagnetic wave carries the least energy?
x: Radio waves have the lowest frequency (longest wavelength) of these, and photon energy E = hν is smallest for the lowest frequency.

q: Compared with a photon of violet light, a photon of red light has:
o: Less energy and a longer wavelength
More energy and a longer wavelength
Less energy and a shorter wavelength
More energy and a shorter wavelength
x: Red light has a longer wavelength and lower frequency than violet light, so each red photon carries less energy (E = hc/λ).

q: What is the frequency of radiation whose photons each carry 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J? (Planck's constant = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
x: ν = E/h = 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ = 1 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Multiplying E by h instead of dividing gives the meaningless 4.4 × 10⁻⁵².

q: Light of frequency 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz delivers a total of 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ J to a detector. With h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, the number of photons received is:
x: Energy of one photon = hν = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5 × 10¹⁴ = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Number = 6.6 × 10⁻¹⁷ / 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 200.

q: The energy of a photon in terms of its wave number ν̄ is:
x: Wave number ν̄ = 1/λ, so E = hc/λ = hcν̄. Energy is directly proportional to wave number.

q: In a vacuum, photons of X-rays and of visible light differ in frequency but have the same:
x: All photons travel at the speed of light, 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, in a vacuum. Energy, wavelength and wave number all depend on frequency, so they differ.

q: Lines produced when excited electrons of hydrogen drop to n = 2 are seen in which part of the spectrum?
x: Transitions ending at n = 2 form the Balmer series, which lies in the visible region. Those ending at n = 1 (Lyman) are ultraviolet.

q: The energy of the electron in the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is −1312 kJ mol⁻¹. The ionisation energy of hydrogen is therefore:
x: Ionisation takes the electron from n = 1 (−1312 kJ mol⁻¹) to infinity (0), so 1312 kJ mol⁻¹ must be supplied; ionisation energy is positive.

q: Electrons falling to the fourth orbit (n = 4) of hydrogen from higher orbits produce the:
x: The series are named by the lower orbit: n = 1 Lyman, 2 Balmer, 3 Paschen, 4 Brackett, 5 Pfund.

q: In Bohr's model, the energy of an electron in any orbit is given a negative value because:
o: Zero energy is taken at infinite distance, and energy is released as the electron is bound
The electron carries a negative charge
The electron loses energy continuously while moving
Energy is absorbed when the electron comes close to the nucleus
x: A free electron at infinity is given zero energy. When it is attracted into an orbit, energy is given out, so its energy in the atom is below zero.

q: Hydrogen atoms are excited so that their electrons reach n = 4. As they return to the ground state, the maximum number of different spectral lines possible is:
When the electron of a hydrogen atom is promoted to an outer orbit, its total energy:
o: Stays the same in every orbit
x: Eₙ = −1312/n² kJ mol⁻¹, so a larger n gives a smaller negative value, i.e. a higher energy. It stays negative while the electron is bound.

q: Which was a limitation of Bohr's atomic model?
o: It could not explain the line spectrum of hydrogen
It could not account for the stability of the hydrogen atom
It could not explain the spectra of atoms having more than one electron
It could not calculate the radius of hydrogen's first orbit
x: Bohr's model worked for hydrogen and one-electron ions, including the orbit radius and the line spectrum, but failed for multi-electron atoms.

q: How many orbitals are present in a p subshell?
x: For l = 1, m can be −1, 0 or +1, giving three p orbitals (px, py, pz). An s subshell has 1, d has 5 and f has 7.

q: A general formula giving how many orbitals any subshell contains, in terms of l, is:
x: m runs from −l to +l, which is 2l + 1 values, each one orbital: s 1, p 3, d 5, f 7.

q: Which pair of orbitals belongs to the same subshell?
x: 3px and 3pz have the same n (3) and l (1), so both are in the 3p subshell. The other pairs differ in n or in l.

q: The quantum mechanical (wave-mechanical) model of the atom, from which the orbital concept comes, is based on the wave equation of:
x: Schrödinger's wave equation, solved for the electron in an atom, gives the orbitals as regions of electron probability. Bohr used fixed circular orbits instead.

q: The orbital concept is needed because a moving electron behaves both as a particle and as a wave. This dual nature of the electron was proposed by:
x: de Broglie suggested that moving particles such as electrons have wave properties (λ = h/mv). Heisenberg gave the uncertainty principle.

q: Which subshell contains the largest number of orbitals?
x: The number of orbitals depends on l, not n: f has 7, d has 5, p has 3 and s has 1.

q: How many atomic orbitals contain at least one electron in a ground-state sodium atom (Z = 11)?
x: Na is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. Occupied orbitals: 1s, 2s, three 2p and 3s = 6. Four is the number of occupied subshells, not orbitals.

q: The number of sub-levels (subshells) in the fourth principal energy level (n = 4) is:
x: Shell n contains n sub-levels: n = 4 has 4s, 4p, 4d and 4f. Sixteen is its number of orbitals and 32 its maximum number of electrons.

q: Which quantum number describes the orientation of an orbital in space?
x: m gives the orientation of an orbital, e.g. px, py, pz. n gives the shell and size, l the shape, and s the spin of the electron.

q: An electron with n = 4 and l = 0 is present in the:
x: l = 0 means an s subshell (l = 1 p, 2 d, 3 f), and n = 4 gives the fourth shell, so it is 4s.

q: Within the same principal energy level of a many-electron atom, the energies of the sub-levels are in the order:
x: In a many-electron atom, sub-levels of the same shell increase in energy as l increases: s < p < d < f. They are equal only in hydrogen.

q: An electron occupies a 3d orbital. Its four quantum numbers (n, l, m, s) could be:
x: For 3d, n = 3 and l = 2, so m can be −2 to +2. l = 3 is not allowed when n = 3, l = 1 would be a p orbital, and m = +3 is impossible when l = 2.

q: Which statement correctly relates principal energy levels, sub-levels and orbitals?
o: An orbital contains several sub-levels, each with its own energy
A sub-level contains several principal energy levels
Each principal energy level contains exactly one orbital
A principal energy level contains sub-levels, and each sub-level contains one or more orbitals
x: The hierarchy is shell (n) → sub-levels (s, p, d, f) → orbitals (1, 3, 5, 7). For example, n = 2 has 2s and 2p, and 2p has three orbitals.

q: How many electrons of an atom could share the values n = 4 and m = 0?
x: For n = 4, l = 0, 1, 2, 3 and each l has exactly one orbital with m = 0. That is 4 orbitals × 2 electrons = 8.

q: The two lobes of a pz orbital lie along the:
o: Line between the x- and y-axes
x: Each p orbital is named after the axis along which its two lobes point, so pz lies along the z-axis.

q: Compared with a 2p orbital, a 3p orbital has:
o: A spherical shape and a larger size
The same size but a different orientation only
The same dumbbell shape but a larger size and higher energy
A dumbbell shape but a smaller size and lower energy
x: All p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped; as n increases from 2 to 3, the orbital becomes larger and higher in energy.

q: Each shell has only one s orbital. This is because for l = 0:
o: The spin quantum number has only one value
The principal quantum number must be 1
The magnetic quantum number has only one value, m = 0
The magnetic quantum number has three values
x: When l = 0, m can only be 0, so there is one orientation. A sphere looks the same in every direction, so one s orbital fits this.

q: The total number of lobes in the three 2p orbitals of an atom taken together is:
x: Each p orbital has two lobes, and there are three p orbitals (px, py, pz), giving 3 × 2 = 6 lobes.

q: The number of spherical (radial) nodes in a 3s orbital is:
x: An s orbital has (n − 1) spherical nodes: 1s has none, 2s one and 3s two.

q: An electron has n = 3 and l = 1. The shape of the orbital it occupies is:
x: l = 1 is a p orbital (here 3p), which is dumbbell-shaped. l = 0 would be spherical, and l = 2 a d orbital.

q: A node in an orbital is a point, surface or plane where:
o: The probability of finding the electron is greatest
The probability of finding the electron is zero
The electron has its highest energy
Two orbitals of different shells overlap
x: A node is a region of zero electron density. For example, the nucleus lies in the nodal plane of a p orbital.

q: The German word Aufbau, used for the rule of filling orbitals, means:
x: Aufbau means building up: electrons are added one by one into orbitals of increasing energy.

q: According to the Aufbau order, the subshell that is filled immediately after 3d is:
x: The order runs …3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s… After 3d (n + l = 5) comes 4p (also 5, but higher n). 4s is filled before 3d.

q: The (n + l) value of a 4f subshell is:
x: For 4f, n = 4 and l = 3, so n + l = 7. This is why 4f fills after 6s (n + l = 6).

q: A student writes the ground-state configuration of beryllium (Z = 4) as 1s² 2s¹ 2p¹. This breaks:
x: The 2s orbital is lower in energy and must be filled before 2p, so the correct ground state is 1s² 2s². No orbital holds two same-spin electrons, so Pauli is not broken.

q: An orbital can hold at most two electrons. This limit follows directly from:
x: Electrons in one orbital share n, l and m, so by Pauli they must differ in spin. Only two spin values exist, so at most two electrons fit.

q: In the ground state of carbon (Z = 6), the two 2p electrons are:
o: In different 2p orbitals with parallel spins
In different 2p orbitals with opposite spins
x: By Hund's rule, electrons enter degenerate 2p orbitals singly with parallel spins before pairing, so carbon has two unpaired electrons.

q: Which pair of subshells has the same (n + l) value?
x: 3d: 3 + 2 = 5 and 4p: 4 + 1 = 5. The others are 4 and 5, 4 and 5, and 4 and 5.

q: Which subshell is filled immediately before 4f?
x: The order is …5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p. 6s has n + l = 6 and 4f has n + l = 7, so 6s fills just before 4f.

q: The electronic configuration of calcium (Z = 20) is:
x: After argon (18 electrons), the next two go into 4s, which is lower in energy than 3d, giving [Ar] 4s².

q: Phosphorus (Z = 15) has how many half-filled 3p orbitals in its ground state?
x: P is [Ne] 3s² 3p³. By Hund's rule the three 3p electrons occupy the three 3p orbitals singly, so all three are half-filled.

q: An atom has the ground-state configuration [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s². Its atomic number is:
x: 18 (argon core) + 10 + 2 = 30, which is zinc.

q: The total number of electrons in p orbitals of an argon atom (Z = 18) is:
x: Ar is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶. The p electrons are 2p⁶ + 3p⁶ = 12.

q: Which species does NOT have the same electronic configuration as argon (Z = 18)?
x: K⁺, Ca²⁺ and S²⁻ each have 18 electrons, like argon. Na⁺ has 10 electrons, the configuration of neon.

q: The number of electrons in the third shell (n = 3) of an iron atom (Z = 26) is:
x: Fe is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s². The third shell holds 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ = 14 electrons.

q: When a copper atom (Z = 29) loses one electron, the configuration of the ion formed is:
x: Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹, and the 4s electron is lost first, so Cu⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰.

q: Which ion has the configuration [Ar] 3d⁵? (Cr = 24, Mn = 25, Fe = 26, Co = 27)
x: Mn is [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s²; losing the two 4s electrons gives Mn²⁺ = [Ar] 3d⁵. Cr²⁺ is 3d⁴, Fe²⁺ 3d⁶ and Co²⁺ 3d⁷.
